title: Closing the Gratitude Gap
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership distinguishes appreciation from praise: praise recognizes results, while appreciation recognizes the effort, character, and sacrifice behind them, even when results fall short. Despite most leaders believing they're good at this, surveys reveal a persistent 'gratitude gap,' with only about a third of employees feeling genuinely appreciated. The piece argues that visible, effortful demonstrations of gratitude land far more powerfully than verbal thanks alone.
points: Praise rewards outcomes; appreciation honors the effort, integrity, and sacrifice behind an attempt, win or lose.
Collapsing appreciation into praise means people are only recognized when results are good — exactly when appreciation matters least.
Only about a third of team members report feeling appreciated by their leader, despite most leaders believing they excel at it.
Demonstrated appreciation (a handwritten note, showing up, a tangible gesture) registers as more sincere than a verbal thank-you.
Leaders should build small, recurring, visible moments of individualized appreciation into their calendars rather than relying on felt-but-unexpressed gratitude.
quotes: Often confused with praise or compliments, appreciation acknowledges effort and character, not outcomes or performance.
A team member can miss a target and still deserve appreciation for the persistence, integrity, or sacrifice they brought to the attempt.
Only about a third of team members say they feel appreciated by their leader.
A verbal “thank you” tends to be treated as politeness, whereas appreciation that requires visible effort or sacrifice from the leader is viewed as far more sincere
Gratitude that costs a leader nothing will typically be remembered as nothing.
